extracted.intended_audience: aspiring Renaissance courtiers / gentlemen (readers seeking ideals of courtly conduct and accomplishments)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance describing the personal qualities, learned accomplishments, arts, manners, and practical use of accomplishments that constitute an exemplary courtier in a Renaissance court. Focuses on what to learn, how to comport oneself, and when/how to deploy accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning in the humanities and languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Be more than 'passably accomplished in letters' — versed in the humanities, conversant with Latin and Greek, well versed in poets, orators, and historians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'let him be more than passably accomplished in letters... conversant not only with the Latin language but with the Greek.' Rationale: knowledge of many excellent writings provides pleasures, themes for praise, and helps preserve glory. Examples: Scipio, Xenophon, Hannibal's acquaintance with Greek. Anti-pattern: those who think letters injurious to arms (the 'French' criticism). Also allows pragmatic restraint if other occupations prevent perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficiency in writing (verse and prose), including vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: Be proficient in writing verse and prose, especially in the vernacular tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'proficient in writing verse and prose, especially in this vulgar tongue of ours.' Benefits: enjoyment, entertainment of ladies, exercise that sharpens judgment of others' works. Scoring notes: if perfection is not reached, suppress poor writings (see separate criterion) but maintain the practice for discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency and confident speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should make the courtier fluent and confident in speaking with everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'these studies will also make him fluent, and... confident and assured in speaking with everyone.' Source: quote of Aristippus to the tyrant. Benefit: social ease and persuasive capacity at court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and cautious self-assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Be diffident rather than forward; avoid falsely persuading oneself of knowledge one does not possess; modestly disclaim praise rather than accept it too openly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'he should be always on his guard, and diffident rather than forward... keep from falsely persuading himself that he knows that which he does not know' and 'let him as it were disclaim [praise] modestly.' Anti-patterns: those who accept praise unreservedly, or who take black for white. Practical note: even if praise is true, protest modestly and emphasize arms as chief profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true friends from flatterers; resist flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize danger of flattery; prefer truthful friends who admonish over flatterers who praise falsely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'books were written showing in what way the true friend may be distinguished from the flatterer.' Explanation: ears love praise and may cause shipwreck; many perceive they are flattered yet love the flatterer. Practical implication: cultivate judgment to detect and discount flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary competence in arms balanced with learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The courtier should be skilled in arms and view other accomplishments as ornaments to arms (though some argue for the reverse); ideally join both accomplishments and have each aid the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate present: Count favors arms as chief (practice of arms pertains to mind and body), Bembo argues letters are superior in dignity. Guidance: combine arms and learning; present arms as chief profession in social presentation to avoid affectation. Example: contest analogies where defenders use their respective 'weapons' (arms or letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation between soldier/learned identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insist on seeming soldier in learning or learned among soldiers; avoid affectation so middling accomplishments seem great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'let him not act like those who insist on seeming soldiers in learning, and learned men among soldiers.' Benefit: authenticity avoids ridicule and makes modest attainments appear greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical skill and its cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be a musician: read notes and play diverse instruments; music is a necessary accomplishment and solace in leisure and court life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'I am not content with the Courtier unless he be also a musician... be able to read notes, he can play upon divers instruments.' Rationale/examples: music soothes the troubled spirit, pleases ladies, shapes habit of mind toward virtue, useful for both peace and war (Alexander, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Lycurgus, Epaminondas). Anti-pattern: dismissal as vanity. Practical note: taught from childhood; tames wild beasts, used in temples and daily toil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and practice of drawing and painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Know how to draw and have acquaintance with the art of painting; painting is an honorable liberal art and useful (e.g., drawing places, fortresses) and enhances appreciation of beauty and proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'this is to know how to draw and to have acquaintance with the very art of painting.' Rationale: ancient precedent (Greeks forbade teaching to slaves), utility in war (maps, sites, bridges), capacity to judge statues, vases, buildings, and symmetry of living bodies. Examples: anecdotes of ancient esteem for painters (Apelles, Protogènes, Metrodorus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to judge works of art and appreciate ancient masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use knowledge of arts to judge merit of statues, vases, buildings, medals, cameos, intaglios, and to appreciate ancient and modern works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'if he should never derive from it other use or pleasure than the help it affords in judging the merit of statues... it also enables him to appreciate the beauty of living bodies.' Benefit: refined taste and cultural capital; examples include anecdotes about ancient patrons and painters (Alexander and Apelles, Zeuxis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress immature work; share only with trusted friends
rubrics_metrics.description: If one cannot reach high perfection in writing or art, one should suppress such work and show it only to a trusted friend to avoid ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'if other occupations or want of study prevent his reaching such perfection... let him be careful to suppress them so that others may not laugh at him, and let him show them only to a friend whom he can trust.' Practical implication: protect reputation; use practice as private exercise to develop judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deploy accomplishments in the right manner, time, and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice accomplishments in appropriate ways, at the right times and manners; many praiseworthy things become inappropriate when practiced out of season, while little things can be highly esteemed if used opportunely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompted by Giuliano: 'declare in what way this and the other accomplishments... are to be practised, and at what time and in what manner.' Practical guidance: discerning opportuneness and context-sensitivity in display and use of skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation of beauty beyond corporeal features
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that pleasure from another derives not only from outward beauty but also from manners, knowledge, speech, gesture, and chiefly the consciousness of being loved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'Many other causes also inflame our minds, besides beauty: such as manners, knowledge, speech, gesture... above all, the consciousness of being loved.' Implication: cultivate whole personhood, not only external features.
